 Stocks slide to kick off major week for Wall Street
 By John Towfighi 
 Updated Nov 16, 2026, 5:04 PM ET 
 PUBLISHED Nov 16, 2026, 4:57 PM ET 
 A trader looks at a monitor as he works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City on November 16, 2026. Wall Street stocks fell Monday as investors approached a pivotal week for artificial intelligence, with earnings due from scandal-hit chip giant Nvidia and the market debut of Anthropic. 
 Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

 New York  —  
 A major week for Wall Street started on a down note. US markets closed lower Monday, led by declines in technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence boom.
 The S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739 points, or 1.4%. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged 19%.
 Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) dropped 4.1%, falling for the third consecutive day since Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia shares are coming off their worst week in 19 months. Investors are gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, expected Tuesday after the market close.
 Shares of the semiconductor chip designer have had a rocky few weeks, with the Huang scandal accelerating declines. Nvidia shares are down roughly 35% since a record high on October 6, erasing about $2 trillion in market value.
 On Monday, shares of Nvidia closed at $156.14, their lowest level since July 1, 2025. Nvidia shares have erased all of their gains over the past 16 months. Nvidia stock was hit by a raft of Wall Street analysts slashing their price targets last week. At Evercore ISI, analysts cut their price target to $186, down from a prior target of $465. At HSBC, analysts cut their target to $170, down from $365.
 Shares of semiconductor chipmakers, Big Tech and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell Monday. Intel shares ( INTC ) fell 7.1%, while Alphabet shares ( GOOG ) fell 3.85%. CoreWeave shares ( CRWV ) sank 6.1%.
 The Commerce Department on Monday also tightened export controls designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips. The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes, such as China, Iran and Russia.
 The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained more than 2% last week. The declines on Monday ate away at those gains. Overall, the S&P and Nasdaq are down roughly 5% and 11%, respectively, since record highs on October 6. The Dow is down 5% since its peak on August 5.
 Investors are also gearing up for Anthropic’s expected initial public offering later this week. The AI frontier lab is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion , and its IPO is a pivotal moment for the tech boom that has become a driving force for the US stock market.
 “How investors view Nvidia’s updates against the recent turmoil left in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure and the market reaction to Anthropic becoming a public company may determine whether the AI trade can gain its footing or whether hiccups here cause further damage across the ecosystem,” Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, wrote in a Monday note.
 This story has been updated with additional content.
